target_customer: State and local criminal justice agencies (corrections, probation and parole) that pay for or receive data tools; philanthropy funds much of the work
problem: Criminal justice data sits in silos and is stale by the time it is compiled, so agencies cannot see what is working or who is eligible for release or supervision changes.
business_model: Nonprofit; open-source data platform and products provided to government agencies, funded by philanthropy and earned revenue from agency partners
product_category: GovTech data platform for criminal justice

founders.name: Clementine Jacoby
education: Stanford University, class of 2015 (per Stanford Daily caption)
founders.background_notes: Worked as a product manager at Google on augmented mobile games; taught dance at a prison while at Stanford, per the Stanford Daily, 2021.

founders.name: Joshua Essex
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as former Principal Engineer and Architect at Opower.

founders.name: Andrew Warren
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder on recidiviz.org about page; no background found.

technical_complexity.rationale: Ingesting, linking and standardizing data from many state agency systems with inconsistent formats is hard integration work, but it uses standard data engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Agency data integrations, government trust and nonprofit status are slow to replicate; the platform is open source, which limits code level defensibility.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent was found building the same wedge as a nonprofit; none acquired or copied it in sources found.

market_need_then: Agencies lacked usable data; Recidiviz reported working with 30 states during COVID-19, whose users released about 40,000 people early, per the Stanford Daily in 2021, which shows need after founding.

branding.name_origin: A play on recidivism; Clementine Jacoby has said the name reflects that concept while arguing the metric is weak (via search summary of a Medium piece, not opened).
branding.domain_note: Uses recidiviz.org, consistent with its nonprofit status.

identity.voice_and_tone: Mission driven, perspective of people affected by the justice system

branding.brand_signature: A nonprofit YC company with no equity held by anyone, per founder interviews
branding.community_and_virality: Press coverage of the CEO includes Forbes 30 Under 30, TIME, Freakonomics and Stanford Daily, per search results; no merch or fan evidence.

brand_strength.rationale: Distinctive name tied directly to the mission and strong founder press, but the name is hard to spell and the founder has criticized the underlying term.

outcome_analysis: Recidiviz grew from a Google volunteer project into a nonprofit with about 120 staff and agency partnerships in about 20 states, aided by philanthropic funding. Founders with data and product skills and pandemic urgency for early release data helped adoption. The nonprofit model avoids venture rounds, so success shows in reach and grants rather than equity valuations.
notes: Nonprofit, so no equity rounds. Grant records from aggregators (about 30 to 36 million in grants from dozens of funders; a 300,000 dollar Schmidt grant in 2021; National Philanthropic Trust 4.5 million) conflict and were not opened at the source, so they are not recorded as rounds. A grantable-type aggregator claimed a 150K YC seed, unverified. Sources disagree on founding year (2018 or 2019). Origin story post was short and gave no history. No competitor with a source dated at or before the 2019 batch was found; a search surfaced only undated or later vendor pages such as Quaro by RS21. Outcome search found no acquisition, layoffs or shutdown for Recidiviz. Name origin comes from a search summary of a Jacoby piece.
